Merchandise
MER-chan-dize
noun; verb
From the Old French marchandise, through Latin mercari, to trade, and merx, wares; hence goods bought and sold, and the act of trading in them. Scripture uses both the honest sense and the sense of trafficking in what must never be sold.

Biblical Definition

Merchandise is goods bought and sold, and by extension the trade itself. Scripture honours it. The virtuous woman of Proverbs 31 is a trader: “She perceiveth that her merchandise is good: her candle goeth not out by night” (Pro 31:18) — she buys a field, plants a vineyard, makes fine linen and delivers girdles to the merchant, and she is praised for it in a chapter which is the Bible’s fullest portrait of an excellent wife. Wisdom herself is commended by the figure: “the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver” (Pro 3:14), which assumes that trade in silver is a real and understood good. Lawful calling in commerce is honest labour under God, and the eighth commandment stands behind every fair sale. But the word turns black in three places. It is forbidden to make merchandise of a person: the captive woman may not be sold (Deu 21:14), and the man-stealer who maketh merchandise of his brother shall die (Deu 24:7). It is forbidden in the house of God: Christ, with a scourge of small cords, drove out the sellers, saying, “make not my Father’s house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16). And it is the last cargo of Babylon, whose merchants weep because no man buyeth their merchandise any more (Rev 18:11), a lading that ends with slaves and the souls of men. Trade is lawful; the traffic in worship and in souls is not.

Webster 1828 Definition

The wares of trade and the trading itself; honoured as lawful calling, forbidden absolutely in the traffic of souls and in the house of God.

MERCHANDISE, n. [French marchandise; L. merx, wares.] The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.

Trade; traffic; commerce; the act of buying and selling.

v. i. To trade; to carry on commerce.

To make merchandise of a person is to traffic in him — forbidden Deu 24:7 on pain of death.

Applied figuratively to wisdom, whose merchandise is better than that of silver (Pro 3:14).

Key Scripture

Pro 31:18 — "She perceiveth that her merchandise is good: her candle goeth not out by night."

Pro 3:14 — "For the merchandise of it is better than the merchandise of silver, and the gain thereof than fine gold."

Joh 2:16 — "And said unto them that sold doves, Take these things hence; make not my Father's house an house of merchandise."

Deu 24:7 — "If a man be found stealing any of his brethren of the children of Israel, and maketh merchandise of him, or selleth him; then that thief shall die; and thou shalt put evil away from among you."

Modern Corruption

Worship is packaged and sold as a product, and the flock is made merchandise by men who preach for gain; meanwhile the opposite error despises lawful trade as though commerce were itself unclean.

expand to see more

Peter warned that false teachers through covetousness would with feigned words make merchandise of the flock (2Pe 2:3), and the warning has never wanted examples. The prosperity ministries sell anointed cloths, miracle water, and seed-faith covenants; the church-growth industry sells worship itself — the service designed as a product, the singing engineered for its effect on the room, the preaching shaped by what the market will bear and the giving campaign built on the same instincts as a sales funnel. Christ’s scourge fell on men doing something far less brazen: selling doves for sacrifice, a genuine convenience for pilgrims, in the outer court of the temple. If that was enough to make His Father’s house an house of merchandise, the trade conducted in His name today is not a lesser thing. Babylon’s manifest ends where such trade always ends — with slaves, and souls of men.

Be evenhanded, for the opposite error is also a corruption. Scripture does not despise commerce. The excellent wife trades and is praised; Lydia sold purple and her house became a church; Paul made tents; private property is guarded by the eighth commandment and the landmark law. A piety that treats business as second-class, or treats profit as theft by definition, has left the Bible for another book. The rule is simply this: sell honestly in the market, with just weights and a kept word, and sell nothing in the sanctuary. Wares are for the market; worship, the ministry of the Word, and the souls of men are not for sale at any price.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The wares and the trading; a lawful calling under God, and an abomination when the goods are worship or men.

expand to see more

Merchandise — Old French marchandise; Latin merx, wares, and mercari, to trade.

Hebrew sachar (to travel about trading) and 'amar (Deu 24:7, to deal tyrannously with).

Greek emporion (Joh 2:16, a place of traffic) and emporeuomai (2Pe 2:3, to make gain of).

Pro 31:18 and Pro 3:14 set the honourable sense; Joh 2:16 and Deu 24:7 the forbidden.

Rev 18:11–13 closes the theme: Babylon’s cargo ends in slaves and souls of men.

Usage

"The word is morally neutral until you ask what is being sold and where."

"Joh 2:16 governs the sanctuary; Pro 31:18 governs the market. Do not swap them."

"“Make merchandise of” in Deu 24:7 and 2Pe 2:3 always means trafficking in persons or souls."
